topic.title: We read the EMI, not the loan
topic.claim: We'll compare two apps for twenty minutes over ₹40, then sign a home loan where a longer tenure quietly adds lakhs.
topic.moment: The bank says 'we can bring the EMI down if we stretch it to 25 years' and everyone at the table relaxes.

turn.believed: A lower EMI means the loan got cheaper.
turn.actually: A longer tenure usually means far more interest overall, and the bank earns more from it.

topic.because: We feel the EMI every month, but the total interest is a number we never see on one screen. Banks sell the comfortable monthly figure.
topic.payoff: Before you sign, ask for the total you'll pay over the full loan. Then decide if the low EMI still feels good.
topic.behaviour: Buyers pick longer tenures to fit EMIs; banks offer tenure stretches as a favour.
topic.mechanism: Monthly comfort hides the total cost, which is where the bank earns.
topic.group: First-time home buyers, late 20s to early 30s
topic.send_to: The couple in your life who is about to book their first flat.
topic.why_now: With flats costing a decade or more of salary, longer loans are becoming the default.

score.why: We compare apps over ₹40 and then take the low EMI of a longer loan. It's a dark pattern with a test the reader can run before signing.

topic.villain: a loan-tenure structure that hides the total interest behind a low EMI
